content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, Babel/Babylon functions as the archetypal symbol of human pride, self-exaltation, and organized rebellion against God — the 'city of man' or godless world system standing in deliberate contrast to the city of God (Jerusalem/Zion). Babel represents humanity's attempt to make a name for itself and reach heaven by its own power (resulting in confusion and scattering), and Babylon extends this into the image of an idolatrous, oppressive, seductive world power destined for divine judgment. In Revelation, 'Babylon the great' is the culminating symbol of this anti-God civilization, whose fall is contrasted with the descent of the New Jerusalem.","primary_basis":["Genesis 11:1–9 (the Tower of Babel: 'let us make a name for ourselves')","Genesis 10:8–10 (Nimrod and the founding of Babel)","Isaiah 13–14 (oracle against Babylon; the taunt against its proud king)","Isaiah 21:9 ('Fallen, fallen is Babylon')","Isaiah 47 (Babylon as the arrogant, humiliated queen)","Jeremiah 50–51 (judgment on Babylon; 'flee from the midst of Babylon')","Daniel 1–5 (Babylon as the proud empire humbled; Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, the writing on the wall)","2 Kings 24–25 / Psalm 137 (Babylon as the power of exile and oppression)","Revelation 14:8; 16:19; 17:1–18; 18:1–24 (Babylon the great, mother of harlots; her fall)","1 Peter 5:13 (the church 'in Babylon,' widely read as symbolic)","Revelation 21–22 (New Jerusalem as the deliberate counter-image)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Babylon in Revelation and 1 Peter as a cipher for the Roman Empire / the city of Rome — the persecuting imperial power of the first century (the historical-critical and much patristic reading; the 'seven hills' of Revelation 17:9).","basis":["Revelation 17:9,18","1 Peter 5:13","Revelation 18 (commerce and empire imagery)"],"prominence":"dominant"},{"meaning":"Babylon as the end-time or trans-historical 'world system' — a recurring/eschatological economic, political, and religious order opposed to God, not tied to any single city (common in evangelical and idealist interpretation, often combined with the primary meaning).","basis":["Revelation 17–18","Genesis 11:1–9","Isaiah 13–14"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Babel/Babylon as confusion and division of human language and unity, typologically reversed at Pentecost (a common homiletical and patristic typology pairing Genesis 11 with Acts 2).","basis":["Genesis 11:7–9","Acts 2:1–11"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Babylon the great as apostate Jerusalem (the city that killed the prophets), the preterist reading of Revelation.","basis":["Revelation 11:8","Revelation 17–18","Matthew 23:35–37"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Babylon as the Roman Catholic Church / papacy — the classic historicist Protestant identification (Luther, Reformation-era polemic; retained in some traditions such as Seventh-day Adventism).","basis":["Revelation 17:1–6","Revelation 18:4 ('come out of her, my people')"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"A literal rebuilt city of Babylon in Mesopotamia as the seat of the end-time Antichrist (some dispensationalist futurists).","basis":["Revelation 17–18","Zechariah 5:5–11","Jeremiah 50–51 read as unfulfilled"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"1 Peter's 'Babylon' as a literal place (Mesopotamian Babylon or the Egyptian garrison town Babylon) rather than a symbol for Rome.","basis":["1 Peter 5:13"],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is unusually strong cross-traditional agreement on the core symbolism: Babel/Babylon = human pride, idolatrous empire, and the anti-God 'city of man' set against God's city, drawn from Augustine's two-cities framework onward. Disagreement is concentrated almost entirely on the referent of 'Babylon' in Revelation (Rome, Jerusalem, papacy, end-time system, literal rebuilt city), not on the underlying symbolic meaning. The Rome identification is dominant in academic scholarship, while the trans-historical world-system reading is dominant in popular preaching; these are usually treated as compatible layers rather than rivals."}
